speechtext: Mr. Chairman, had the Minister of Transport completed his statement when his estimates were up some weeks ago?

but I feel that the statement was sufficiently complete not to require adding to it further at this time.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO NEW COMMERCIAL ROUTES IN UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the estimates book for the fiscal year 1953-54 indicates that the Department of Transport is the fourth largest spending department. The amount asked for in the estimates as originally tabled is slightly over $110,300,000, and in addition to that the department is asking for nearly $4,500,000 in the supplementary estimates. So the expenditures by this department have a considerable effect on the amount of taxation that must be paid by the Canadian people.
In opening the discussion on his estimates the minister dealt at some length with the summary of standard objects of expenditure and special categories to be found in the folder at the back of the estimates book. This summary approaches the estimates from a different direction in that it summarizes how expenditures are to be made for salaries and wages, travelling and removal expenses and so on.
I must give the minister full marks for taking the trouble to review his estimates on the basis of that summary of standard objects. He has been the only minister in the cabinet to do so during the present session, and it does enable hon. members to get a better view of just how the money of his department is to be spent.
There are five different groups in his department in so far as this summary is drawn. First, the general item described as department; then the air transport board; the board of transport commissioners; the Canadian maritime commission and the national harbours board. When we take them together we find that this year the Department of Transport is asking for an increase over what was spent last year of nearly $8 million, which, together with the supplementary estimates of nearly $5 million, make a total increase for this department of almost $12,500,000. That is the largest increase of any department except finance and national health and welfare. I doubt very much the necessity for the department to ask for an increase of that kind.
In turning to the summary of standard objects to which I referred a few minutes ago, I find where some of these increases are to be made. For example, in the item of "standard objects", which is described as "professional and special services", there is an increase of $319,000 for the present fiscal year. The minister mentioned that, when he spoke on March 12. His reference is found at page 2903 of Hansard. He said that most of that was for an expansion in investigation
[Mr. Chevrier.l
and planning for the St. Lawrence seaway. I hope when he answers he will go into further details and explain just how it comes about that there is that large increase in the item "professional and special services".
Then, another standard object in which there is a very great increase is for telephones, telegrams and other communication services. This year the minister's department is to spend $205,900 more than was spent last year for these services. That is a lot of money, particularly when we consider that this department spends far more than any other department except the Department of National Defence under telephones, telegrams and other communication services. I suggest to the minister that he have his officials take another look at these expenditures for telephones, telegrams and other communication services. He may find that there is considerable picking up of the phone to send messages by long distance which could have been sent free under the franking privilege of his department.
Another standard object in which there is a large increase is materials and supplies. The increase there is $372,400. I do not believe that the minister explained satisfactorily why it is necessary to ask for that much additional money. Here again he is asking for a great deal more than most of the other departments. His department is the third or fourth highest in the requirements for materials and supplies.
Then finally with regard to these standard objects there is an increase of over half a million dollars-the figure is $580,974

in what are described as "contributions, grants, subsidies, et cetera, not included elsewhere". When the minister spoke he made no explanation whatever about this increase. The total amount is large, amounting, for the Department of Transport as distinct from the air transport board, the board of transport commissioners, the maritime commission and the national harbours board, to over $11,500,000. I would ask the minister to give us an explanation both of the amount required and of the fact that there is such a large increase in that item, for the present fiscal year.
So much by way of a very brief review of the figures shown in this summary of standard objects. There is one other matter which I wish to place before the committee briefly, that has to do with one of the main fields in which this department is responsible. It is in charge of three main types of transportation in Canada, all of which are of vital importance to the nation. They are, first, water transportation; second, rail transportation; and third, air transportation. It is my Understanding that the dominion government

is not, as yet at least, accepting any responsibility for transportation by highway. My remarks have to do exclusively with transportation by water.
I believe that Canada is now in a new era in so far as transportation by water is concerned, and particularly because of three developments. In the first place on the high seas since the war the business of transportation of goods has been taken over more and more each year by the fast cargo vessels as distinct from the slow old type of freighter which was used during the second world war.
Then, secondly, because of the great increase in oil tankers, I understand that over half of the shipping being built in the world today is in the shape of oil tankers. This is of importance to Canada because on our west coast at least we are shortly to be in the position of having oil brought down from Alberta by pipe line, and we hope that it will be shipped out from Vancouver and New Westminster to other nations of the world.
Some of the oil is going down to the United States by branch pipe line to supply a refinery. I am hoping the oil that is to be exported from the west coast is not going to be exported from American ports instead of Canadian ports. In any event, we are today in no position to carry any of this oil overseas. I think that raises a very important problem for the Department of Transport and I see no reason why Canadian ships cannot be in the business of transporting crude oil from Canadian west coast ports.
The third important development which I submit to the minister is that I believe we are in a new era for water transport in Canada with the proposal to build the St. Lawrence waterway. I read in the press that, according to the minister, there may be two St. Lawrence waterways. He went over the deep end down in the United States the other day and advocated or suggested the possibility of having two waterways.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO NEW COMMERCIAL ROUTES IN UNITED STATES
speechtext: I know that my hon. friend does not want to mislead the house. Two canals and two waterways are two different things. I did suggest, but not advocate, the construction of a canal on the American side and one on the Canadian side. That is not the same as two waterways.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO NEW COMMERCIAL ROUTES IN UNITED STATES
speechtext: Perhaps I should have said two canals. To be technically accurate, the waterway runs all the way from Fort William-

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO NEW COMMERCIAL ROUTES IN UNITED STATES
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO NEW COMMERCIAL ROUTES IN UNITED STATES
speechtext:
-to below Quebec. I will change my remark and say two canals. However, I would be prepared to settle for one and I think most Canadians are of the same
Supply-Transport
opinion. The very fact that the St. Lawrence waterway system is to be developed by either one or two canals, to the extent that there is to be a great deal more shipping coming into the great lakes, means that Canada is facing a new day in water transportation. I am quite confident that the minister will agree with that remark. That brings up the question of whether Canadian ships are going to get the benefit of this new canal and the benefit of the great discoveries of iron ore in Quebec and Labrador, or whether we are going to sit back and let the United States, and perhaps some other nations, beat us out in so far as the carrying trade is concerned.
I envisage the transport of iron ore, or preferably ore in the metal form, for I see no reason why we cannot use the water power in the province of Quebec to make electricity and with it turn a great deal of this iron ore into the metal form before it is exported. However, it is certain that there will be great transportation of iron ore or iron in the metal form through this St. Lawrence waterway system; and very probably Canadian grain will be coming back on the same ships.
Now, where does Canada stand with regard to this new trade? When General McNaughton was before the committee on external affairs he said that half of the shipping going through the new canal would consist of boats carrying iron ore. Incidentally, he said that they did not want fast ships going through the canal because fast ships would make more current and do more damage to the banks of the canal-so they prefer to have slow ships. He also said that he did not think there would be any ships over 10,000 tons so that our hopes of having the Queen Mary dock in Toronto harbour are not likely to be fulfilled. I was quite surprised to learn that there would probably be no ships over 10,000 tons using that new canal.
These three features are at least three of the important features which must be taken into consideration in deciding on a policy for water transport in Canada at this time. The fact that now high seas trade is carried in fast cargo vessels, and that there are greatly increased numbers of oil tankers, and the opening of the St. Lawrence waterway will mean an entirely new day for water transport on that water.
Mr. Chairman, I believe there is grave danger of Canada being left behind in this new water transport field. Our people have a maritime tradition. Right down from the original settling of this country the Canadian people have been followers of the sea

Supp ly-Transport
and of the great inland waterways. Furthermore, we rely on export by water to as great a degree probably as any other nation in the world except the United Kingdom. It is of tremendous importance that Canada should keep up to date in respect of this water transportation. However, where do we stand? What is our position today? I suggest that it is not what it should be. First of all, dealing with the question of fast cargo vessels for the high seas, Canada has practically none of that type of vessel. Just today the Vancouver Sun which came to my desk contains a picture which indicates so clearly what is happening with regard to this high seas traffic. It shows a picture of a ship coming under the bridge over the first narrows in Vancouver harbour. The caption is "Maiden Voyage":
Maiden voyage to port ol Vancouver was made Wednesday by Norwegian freighter Anna Bakke. Vessel which is 6082 tons with speed of 17 knots joins two other Knutsen Line ships in Orient service of company. Under command of Capt. John Fegerland, O.B.E., Anna Bakke is loading lumber and flour.
Now, we used to believe that the old slow war vessels were what was needed for lumber and flour. Yet here we have a case of a fast Norwegian freighter coming into the port of Vancouver to load those two commodities. It is happening every week. Some fast cargo vessel from some other nation is coming into the ports on the west coast and carrying away our products.
A year ago I asked the minister about the possibility of Canada having fast cargo vessels. The discussion took place on May 22, 1952, and at that time, between question and answer, it was determined that Canada had only 57 of the old 10,000 or 7,500 ton slow vessels built during the war. In addition, there were one or two tankers but the bulk of our merchant fleet was made up of those 57 old slow wartime vessels. Also, there were 97 Canadian-owned ships of the same type which were operating under the British flag. By the policy of this government a large number of those slow wartime ships were turned over to British registry, meaning of course that British crews were taken on to replace Canadian crews. I presume there are still a large number of those vessels operating under British registry. I would like the minister to tell us today what the figures are now. How many of those ships have been sold in the meantime, what is the number of vessels registered in Canada, and what is the number of Canadian-owned vessels registered in the United Kingdom?
Several years ago the government was warned about this need for fast cargo vessels

by the Canadian maritime commission. A plan was adopted known as the replacement plan, under which the owner of one of the old slow ships could sell that ship provided he put the proceeds into an escrow fund which was to be used for the purchase of new fast cargo vessels. This scheme has not had the result which was hoped for. I have here the last report of the Canadian maritime commission, dated June 30, 1952. There, we find that all the money in the escrow fund has been used up with the exception of $3-5 million. No doubt more of the money has been spent in the intervening period, and that escrow fund is very much lower now. The report indicates very clearly that the escrow fund has not had the result of bringing about the modernization of the Canadian cargo fleet.
The report tells of the construction of two oil tankers.

speechtext: There is about $6 million in the fund now.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO NEW COMMERCIAL ROUTES IN UNITED STATES
speechtext:
That means, of course, that further ships have been sold in the meantime. The report tells of the construction of two modern tankers, and then we find this paragraph at page 7:
The commission has always been anxious to see the primary purpose of the plan fulfilled through the building of new ocean-going tonnage, and it is to be hoped that the two new tankers will prove to be the forerunners of other ocean-going vessels built in Canadian shipyards.
In the meantime Canada has been building fast cargo vessels for other countries. I believe there are ships of this type on the ways right now to go to other nations. Other countries are forging ahead steadily and rapidly with the building of modern cargo fleets.
I have here the publication Foreign Trade published by the Department of Trade and Commerce. It is dated January 17 of this year, and we find this statement with regard to Japan:
Japan's shipbuilding industry has emerged from the postwar doldrums to become the second most important in the world. In the second quarter of 1952, Japanese construction exceeded that of the United States by a scant margin. Britain, however, continues to lead with a two-million-ton construction program.
Something of a record was established when the Hitachi Shipbuilding and Engineering Company launched three ocean-going vessels on three successive December days, at three different Hitachi dockyards. The three ships were rated at 171, 15J, and 15 knots, with a deadweight tonnage of 10,450, 7,600, and 20 thousand respectively.
Every ship is a fast ship, several knots faster than the type in the Canadian merchant navy. Germany is also building a modern cargo fleet, and Foreign Trade for February 21, 1953, has this to say:
According to latest statistics, in July 1952 gross world tonnage of merchant ships was 90,180,000

tons, an increase of 2,935,000 tons over the previous year. The largest expansions during the year were in Japan, Italy, Germany, Liberia-
Of course, that is because the ship owners from other countries are putting their ships under Liberian registry for tax advantages, I presume.
-France and Sweden. Lloyd's Register figures show that the wartime building program is still reflected in world tonnage by a preponderance of the six to eight thousand ton group, but a large proportion of this is not in commission. Of ships built since the war, the largest volume of tonnage now falls in the ten to fifteen thousand ton group. The marked increase in this group since 1951 is the result of the construction of oil tankers.
In the St. Lawrence area the United States is moving ahead to build vessels which will take trade through the new canal. I believe, Mr. Chairman, that there is an urgent need for a policy which will keep Canada in a position to compete in this water transportation, not only keep us in a position to compete but also to meet the requirements which are resulting from the great developments taking place in this nation such as the development with regard to iron ore and the oil pipe lines. These are developments which call for a new look at Canadian water transportation policy.
A year ago, on June 26, the minister told the house that he had set up a committee to study the question of establishing standard cargo vessels which would meet the requirements of shipping interests and also be adequate for national defence needs in the event of an emergency. Nothing has been heard about that committee in the intervening time. I even hear rumours that the minister now has a committee studying the possibility of going right out of the business of having a Canadian merchant navy and letting the other countries carry on that activity.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO NEW COMMERCIAL ROUTES IN UNITED STATES
speechtext: I might as well say now that there is no truth in that at all.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO NEW COMMERCIAL ROUTES IN UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I am very glad to hear that. I think it would be a great tragedy for Canada if she does not adopt a vigorous water transportation policy. There is one thing the Minister of Transport could do, and that is to strengthen the Canadian maritime commission. This commission was set up in 1947 with the idea of having it supervise water transportation in the same way that the board of transport commissioners supervises rail transportation and that the air transport board supervises air transportation. A very distinguished marine lawyer from Vancouver, Mr. J. V. Clyne, was made chairman of that maritime commission. He and his associates did a remarkable job. They were the ones who recommended policies of different kinds.
Supply-Transport
They reviewed the whole shipping situation in so far as Canada was concerned.
On July 7, 1950, Mr. Clyne was appointed to the bench of the supreme court of British Columbia, and for some months there was no chairman of the commission. Then, on December 30, 1950, the deputy minister of transport was named chairman of the commission. I have great respect for the deputy minister of transport. I think he is a splendid deputy and doing a very worth-while job for Canada. But he has other work to do. It is just as ridiculous as it would be to have the deputy minister of transport act as the chairman of the board of transport commissioners or chairman of the air transport board.
This is a condition which should not be continued. If there is justification for having a Canadian maritime commission, then there should be a proper commission with a chairman having the status of a deputy head, which was the original idea. The commission should be able to go into these questions of policy and make recommendations, spending their full time considering this vitally important problem. Instead of that the commission has been made just one more office in the Department of Transport. I believe that that policy does not do justice either to the men who are trying to do this work or to the people of Canada to whom shipping and transportation by water have always been, and will always be, of such vital importance.

Mr. Chairman, I want to make a few remarks at this time on the first item of the transport estimates in order to deal with rail transportation. It seems to me that the time has now arrived when the government should be giving some thought to a basic change in its transportation policy. The system now followed, that of having the railway companies appear before the board of transport commissioners to ask for additional freight rate increases as a result of certain changed costs, has resulted in such a pyramiding of freight rates that freight rates as to now constitute a serious economic threat to western Canada particularly and also to the maritime provinces. If there is a continuation of the policy of adding one increase in freight rates to another, you are going to get depressed economic areas in Canada because of reduced prices for basic products and increased prices of manufactured products coming into those areas.
Since 1948 we have had freight rate increases totalling 98 per cent. Every time there is an increase in freight rates the producer in western Canada gets less for his product and he is obliged to pay more for

Supply-Transport
manufactured products coming in from eastern Canada. I believe it is time the government considered a subsidy policy with respect to freight rates in order to protect the economic interests of the people in those two main areas of Canada.
The government says it is opposed to subsidies, that it would have to tax the Canadian people in order to get money to pay them. Today freight rates are, in fact, a tax on the persons and on the areas using those facilities. The tax that has resulted from increased freight rates is causing an almost intolerable burden on people in certain areas of Canada. While no one likes taxation of any kind, I nevertheless submit that moneys coming out of the consolidated revenue fund are raised in a much fairer way than are revenues resulting from increases in freight rates. The government has provided some subsidy in this connection. For example, a subsidy is now paid on feed grains moving to eastern Canada. I think that policy should be extended in order to protect the legitimate interests of western Canada and of the maritime provinces. I think that the government should not stand idly by and allow one freight rate increase to follow another. The railways are now getting to the place where, in the higher priced freight traffic, they are pricing themselves out of the market. We have the statement of the president of the Canadian National Railways, Mr. Donald Gordon, to that effect. This was his statement:
We are in a dilemma, and it is getting increasingly worse. With each freight rate award, the area in which we can get an effective increase is narrowing, and we are pricing ourselves out of the market steadily.
Every time there is an increase in freight rates the railway companies price themselves out of a certain market; and when they price themselves out of those markets and their volume of freight traffic is reduced, then of course they soon have to go back to the board of transport commissioners for another increase in freight rates.
Anyone in western Canada now travelling on the highway will see large transport trucks, each transporting four or five automobiles. That business must be a fairly lucrative one or you would not have the trucks taking it away from the railways. We now have a dual system. We have trucks, running alongside the railway lines, pounding the roads to pieces, causing an increasing burden on the taxpayers in any given province who bear the cost of maintaining adequate highways, and we have the railway companies pricing themselves out of the market.
When this matter was being discussed previously during this session, we made the

request of the minister and of the government that they disallow the last increase in freight rates. We received the same reply to that request as we have received to similar requests we have made in the past: The governor in council was not prepared to disallow the freight increase. The minister, however, in that debate, made one statement that I think was rather misleading. It is reported at page 2755 of Hansard and it has to do with the board's dealing with an application of the railway companies for a 7 per cent increase in freight rates following the increase in wage rates. The minister says this:
May I Interrupt my hon. friend to say to him that the effect of the supreme court judgment in the case to which I referred earlier and to which he refers is that when there is an increase in wages it follows that there must be a consequent increase in freight rates.
I think that statement is misleading because it implies that every time wage rates go up there must be a comparable increase in freight rates and that that was the ruling of the supreme court. I have the ruling here, and I do not think that ruling was made in that way at all. What the supreme court has ruled is that when the railway companies apply to the board of transport commissioners for an increase in freight rates-let us say following an increase in wages-the board of transport commissioners must deal with that application and that they cannot-as they did once in the past -postpone dealing with that application until certain studies were made or until certain legislation was passed.
All the ruling says to the board of transport commissioners is this: "When -an application is before you, you must deal with it." But when the application is before the board of transport commissioners, they do not need to say: "Wage rates have gone up $50 million; therefore freight rates must also go up by $50 million." What they have to do is to consider the fact that wage rates have gone up, then consider all other items of cost going into railway operations, any items of savings and, on the basis of all those factors, then decide what is a fair and reasonable freight rate increase.
I therefore say that it does not necessarily follow that every time there is an increase in wage rates the board of transport commissioners is forced to give the same increase in freight rates. I say that board has the right and the duty to take into account all the various cost factors and then to make a ruling on the basis of those various factors.
When the board of transport commissioners is making a ruling as to freight rates, I think it should take into account all the revenue that the Canadian Pacific Railway

obtains. I think they should take into account the revenue the C.P.R. obtains from various investments such as, for instance, investments in hotels, in steamship companies, in mines, in lands, and all of those subsidiary undertakings of the C.P.R. There is a good reason why other income should be taken into account. The public of Canada, through the Canadian government, in the past granted the C.P.R. 25 million. acres of land free and granted the C.P.R. $25 million as a subsidy. Because of these various grants the C.P.R. was placed in a financial position where it could extend its operations to other fields. Just so long as the board-

rate lawyers in their pleas before the transport board for increases in freight rates-the rate base application is an apt illustration. This rate base application if granted in full would hoist rates 30 per cent or about $150 million per year. And it must never be forgotten that the people of western Canada pay the greater part of these increases.
And on the point as to who is paying the freight rate increases I would refer to another article under the heading "Seven Per Cent Freight Rate Boost", written by Shane Mac-Kay for the Sifton papers. In this article I find this very important paragraph:
Freight rate increases fall almost exclusively on traffic to, from and within western Canada. In eastern Canada, most traffic is carried under competitive and special rates originally designed to meet truck and water competition. In the mari-times, the impact is cushioned by a 20 per cent statutory subsidy on a considerable proportion of traffic and by the existence of many arbitrary rates. International rates on traffic moving between Canada and the United States are governed largely by decisions of the interstate commerce commission.
Thus when the railways ask the board for a "general" increase in rates they are asking for higher rates, not in eastern Canada or on international traffic, but largely in the four western provinces. And as each "general" increase is added to the western freight toll, the rate structure becomes more distorted and the burden upon the west heavier.
That sums up very well the effect of increases in freight rates.
People living in the four western provinces are, in the main, those who suffer as a result of increasing freight rates. I am hopeful that the government will re-think its transportation policy, and decide what place subsidies can fill in keeping down the cost of freight rates.
As I say, one can argue against subsidies and against the taxpayers footing any part of the bill for freight; but if it is not done that way you have a freight burden which, in fact, is another form of taxation, an unjust burden that bears most heavily on the people in the four western provinces.
While this matter is before the governor in council, naturally I cannot say anything about it. I am hopeful however that the minister will give this problem his very earnest consideration, that he will consider the situation in western Canada, and that he will do everything in his power to prevent the freight rates burden increasing to those proportions which would cause depressed industries and depressed areas in Canada.

Since the matter has been raised I wanted to put myself on record as emphatically as possible as advocating the importance of this particular payment to the economy of the maritimes.
For a moment I should like to refer to freight rates, with particular reference to the maritime provinces. The hon. member for Assiniboia dealt with this matter effectively, and without necessarily associating myself with all he said I do want to say that in general I agree with him as to the importance of the freight rate problem at the moment. But I do not agree with the quotation which he gave, I think from Shane Mac-Kay, which referred to the Maritime Freight Rates Act as a subsidy for the railroads operating in the maritime provinces.
I suppose in one sense of the word it might be termed a subsidy because the treasury reimburses the railroads for certain payments; but as everyone knows who has any knowledge of the historical background, these railroads were constructed in the years gone by when it was thought that we might be at war with the country to the south. They built a long, narrow, tortuous, twisting railway along the coast line, even going into the constituency of the hon. member for Gloucester, and then going down the St. Lawrence and getting as far away from the

Supply-Transport
United States border as possible, which has resulted in a much longer mileage than was necessary, and therefore heavier freight rates. Because of that and other factors the matter was determined by the Maritime Freight Rates Act many years ago, and I shall refer to that again in a moment.
I do want to agree with my hon. friend in this. The railways have priced themselves out of the competitive short-haul market. They have been raising rates until they have got to the place where the profitable short haul has been taken over by trucks. For instance, the hon. member for Peterborough West told me this morning that in driving up yesterday he passed seven heavy transit trucks hauling automobiles to market, seven on one relatively short stretch of highway. This is traffic which a few years ago was hauled by the railways, but which they have now lost. The result is that the railways are becoming the conveyors of long haul traffic. The increased rates which they have had to impose each year, or which they say they have to impose, have therefore rested very heavily on that long haul.
The position in the maritimes is obvious. We are on the periphery of this dominion, and to get access to the central main markets we have that long haul to make. The result is that the increase in freight rates has rested very heavily upon us, and it is preventing the maritime industries from getting access to this Canadian market.
Twenty-five years ago one W. H. Dennis, now Senator Dennis, of the Halifax Herald, spearheaded a movement for maritime rates, and as a result of that we got the Duncan commission, and we had the Maritime Freight Rates Act, to which I referred a moment ago. That Maritime Freight Rates Act has been of tremendous importance to the maritimes and is still of some assistance; there is no question about that. But because of the competition, the adjustment of the rates to the truck hauls and various factors which have entered into the modern rate structure, the Maritime Freight Rates Act is not of nearly the advantage that it was some time ago. The time has come, Mr. Chairman, when the whole situation should be reviewed again. There needs to be a complete survey of this matter, particularly in so far as its incidence on the maritime freight rates is concerned.

Mr. Chairman, the county of Saguenay, which I have the honour of representing in the house, has experienced a tremendous development in recent years. This is undoubtedly the result of united efforts on the part of capital and labour, as well as of unrelenting initiative on the part of local authorities, both civil and religious, but it is also largely the result of the co-operation offered by the federal government and more particularly by the Department of Transport.
In fact, since 1949, that department has spent large sums of money in my county for the construction of lighthouses, aids to navigation, the paving of runways and improvements to airports, such as at Baie Comeau, Sept lies and Havre St. Pierre. We shall soon be called upon to vote more money for airports at Forestville, Riviere au Tonnerre, Aguanish and Natashquan.
The federal government, and more particularly the Department of Transport, has understood that the Saguenay district represents a great asset for the country and that they should do everything in their power to foster its development as far as possible. Under the circumstances, I deem it my duty, on behalf of my electors, to thank the Minister of Transport and through him, the Canadian government, for their frank and loyal collaboration.
However, my heartfelt thanks should not be interpreted as meaning that we have come to the end of our requests. On the contrary, it calls for further accomplishments. Mr. Speaker, my constituents, though they may be considered as idealists, are nevertheless very practical people. Through generations, they have been able to adapt themselves to a powerful nature, and their forefathers, during three centuries of isolation, had the opportunity to dream of the greatness and the destiny of their country. Yes, indeed, cherishing their land and remembering the past, they are aware of the present and have faith in the future. They know that their district is an empire. They know also that the twentieth century will be the century of the Saguenay as well as the century of Canada. I share that conviction for I am one of them and have been trained at the same

Supply-Transport
school. This feeling is shared also by the newcomers, for they, also, are empire builders. Natural resources of all kinds may be found in the Saguenay district. There is an abundance of water power, forest and mining resources in that district and all that is needed in order to ensure its development for the common good is capital and manpower.
Mr. Chairman, to my mind the Saguenay district will hardly have reached its maturity when all its mineral rich district to the north will have been brought under development, when, instead of being merely a field from which riches are drawn, it will have become, throughout its length and breadth, a huge factory where raw materials will be worked on the spot, when it will have 200,000 people instead of 40,000, when it will have in this Canadian parliament four representatives instead of one.
But when will all this come about? When the Saguenay region will have been equipped with such land communications as are necessary to enable its people to communicate amongst themselves and to carry out commercial transactions with their neighbours from Charlevoix, Chicoutimi and even Newfoundland, when there will be wharves in every one of its main ports, airports in every strategic location, maritime services which will link all its larger centres with the vital points on the south shore of the St. Lawrence, telephone and telegraph lines throughout its length and breadth, when all Her Majesty's subjects will receive, every day, Her Majesty's mail, when, finally, a railway will complete, in a perfect manner, all this communications system.
Mr. Chairman, as I describe this to you, I do not feel I am indulging in any dreams, but rather, on the contrary, that I am faithfully describing what the constituency of Saguenay will be in the latter half of the twentieth century.
Now, as regards the north shore railway, I had occasion, on April 24, 1951, to communicate to this house my views on the subject. But I should like to record today an article by Mr. Gilles Trepanier, civil engineer of Haute Rive (Saguenay), which was published in the March 1953 issue of L'Aquilon, under the title:
A Railway on the North Shore
The north shore could produce annually 4 million cords of pulpwood, 20 million tons of iron ore, 5 million tons of ilmenite; its hydraulic resources could be developed to produce more than 5 million horsepower. The development of all these natural resources is being delayed because there is no railway in the county. Industrial leaders prefer to take the raw materials out of the county and refine them elsewhere, because they have no adequate and reliable transport facilities at their disposal.
In other words, there is no industry in our county through lack of railway, and no railway

through lack of industry. It would be a good thing to break this vicious circle.
In closing my remarks, Mr. Speaker, may I ask the hon. Minister of Transport to establish a commission to study the possibility of undertaking such a project and to give us his views in relation to this problem.

I received recently numerous representations from my electors concerning the two problems about which I would like to say a few words this afternoon.
The first of these problems concerns the Cooperative de transport maritime et aerien, the C.T.M.A. as it is commonly known on the islands. is made with Halifax. At the present time, the situation is such that the co-operative will be unable to look after transportation between the islands and Halifax unless it obtains grants from the government. A request to that effect has already been made to the maritime commission and I am presently seeing that the officials of that commission get all the pertinent information. I am confident that the commission will give favourable consideration to the request and that the hon. minister will do everything in his power so that a grant may be made soon.
The second problem concerns communications proper, or, if you prefer, the telephone system. On the Magdalen islands, as everyone knows, the telephone system is under the jurisdiction of the Department of Transport.
During the war, we had a 24-hour a day service. Since the end of the war, we had been getting no service at all from 10 o'clock at night until the following morning. Recently, however, the hon. minister has been kind enough to authorize a resumption of the 24-hour a day service at the exchange on Grindstone island, the most populous of the Magdalen islands. We are very grateful and we thank the minister. However, there are two more exchanges on the Magdalen islands, one at Grosse lie and the other at Havre Aubert. The exchange at Grosse lie is located at the east end of the Magdalen islands and the one at Havre Aubert, at the west end. The people who live in these places might even have a greater need of telephone service than those who live in Cap-aux-Meules since the hospital and most public services are located there. Indeed the people who live in Havre Aubert and at Grosse lie made representations in order to obtain a 24-hour a day service at those points. This would not mean much of an increase in cost since all it would entail is the addition of two employees in each place. I have made a request myself along that line and I trust that the minister will give this request particular attention.
Then, again, there is the problem of long distance telephone service. Some two years ago a radiotelephone system was installed to enable the inhabitants of the islands to communicate with the mainland. The apparatus was operated for a few months but since it was not satisfactory it was taken out for repairs. We would have liked them to be in working order this year before the fishing season. Unfortunately such is not the case. I leave the matter to the minister. I believe the Magdalen islanders can trust him to give this problem special consideration and that we will receive good news in this connection.

I am not criticizing him for the statement he made today, but if by any chance I am wrong, then I still say it should not be transferred to national defence. However, despite the improvement that those employees have enjoyed, the fact remains that there are still 3,206 retired employees of the C.N.R. whose only pension from the railway is the $25 a month basic pension. The subject matter of this question was fully discussed last year in this house and in the railway committee. The reasons were given in the discussion which took place and no representations were received from the management of the Canadian National Railway's on this question.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure we all realize that the estimates of the Department of Transport invite the consideration of a large number of subjects, but we also are aware of the urgency of getting through the estimates as quickly as possible. I shall confine my remarks to three or four matters which I consider important enough to bring to the attention of the committee and the minister at this time.
I believe the minister has received from the Secretary of State the representations which have been made by a large number of employees of the Canadian National Railways in Newfoundland regarding their rights to pension under the terms of union between Canada and Newfoundland. The letter sent to the Secretary of State, which he forwarded to the Minister of Transport, indicated that prior to 1949 these servants of the railroad and the postal and telegraph departments were eligible for pension under the Civil Service Act of Newfoundland of 1926.
Under one of the terms of union it was provided that civil servants would not have their positions worsened through confederation. However, since 1949 while persons formerly employed in other departments of the government in Newfoundland who have continued in the employ of the province of Newfoundland or of the federal government have become entitled to pensions, those employed by the Canadian National Railways and the telegraph system have had their rights ignored. This is a most important matter affecting 4,000 employees. I trust that since the minister received the letter from the Secretary of State he has been able to give consideration to this matter and is now in a position to make a pronouncement, either today or very soon.
The other matter to which I wish to refer is in connection with freight rates. I have brought this matter to the attention of the minister before. It has to do with the award which was made in favour of Newfoundland to the effect that that province was entitled to benefits under the Maritime Freight Rates Act. I pointed out that the award stated that under the terms of union Newfoundland was entitled to those benefits and should have received them as of April 1, 1949. However,

Newfoundland did not receive those benefits until after the award had been given. Therefore the government of Newfoundland and the people of Newfoundland submit, and I contend rightly, that they have been charged enormous sums, running into the millions of dollars, by way of the excessive rates which they paid prior to the date of the award.
The next question concerns the matter of the Newfoundland dockyard. Last year the management paid off 86 employees, and there was a rumour that the dockyard was going to close down altogether. The dockyard has been a very important source of employment for the tradesmen in St. John's West since the first dock was built about 80 years ago, and it seems to me that a lack of interest on the part of somebody is responsible for work not being passed along to the dock. With all the work that is going ahead now in the Dominion of Canada that requires work by boilermakers and machinists of various kinds, one would think there would be some work passed along to the dockyard in St. John's to be handled there. I believe that our men down there are as competent as you will find in any other part of the Dominion of Canada. It seems to me to be unfair to men who have been working at trades for so long to have to live in fear of unemployment on account of the dockyard being closed down. As the minister knows, in the hearing before the committee there was some question of passing it over to some private enterprise. The government should make some effort to operate the dockyard itself.

Instead of going into great detail, sir, I am going to read the letter from the Canadian National Railways veterans' association of Saskatoon, written on February 22, 1953, in which the question is set forth in detail and in essence but without unnecessary wording. It reads as follows:
I have been instructed by resolution, unanimously passed at the last regular meeting of this association, February 17, 1953, to write to the members of parliament expressing our hope that they will exercise their influence on the federal government in an effort to bring some relief to the retired railway employees who are receiving only the basic pension of $25 per month.
We have made requests through our former labour organizations, as well as appealing to the management of the railways, in an effort to obtain a measure of relief for the pensioners in the very low pay brackets but have been unsuccessful in each attempt, so there is no other course than to appeal to the government and to the parliament of the Dominion of Canada in an effort to have justice done to those of our members in the lower salary brackets who through no fault of their own were unable to contribute to the voluntary pension plan, effective January 1, 1935.
We are not asking further consideration for our members in the higher salary brackets who could have contributed but did not do so, but we are appealing to you and to the government for simple justice for our members who, through no fault of their own, were unable to contribute to the pension fund . . . during the depression years-
I will omit several paragraphs which are merely in support of the argument, but there is this vital and cogent passage:
The pioneer railroad man in Canada worked long hours under the most trying and difficult conditions which should entitle him to at least fair consideration by the government in the matter of pension payments regardless of the period of time within which the services were rendered.
Finally they say that many of these men were discharged during the thirties when
IMr. Diefenbaker.]
employment was uncertain and when their rate of wage was such that they were unable to make a contribution.
I should also like to put on the record the representations of the retired railway veterans association of Alberta made on January 25, 1953, requesting that some consideration be given to those receiving the basic pension of $25 per month. They point out that in the western region of the Canadian National Railways there are 5,000 pensioners and quite a number, especially those in the lower wage brackets, were unable to contribute to the pension plan. They say in part:
Donald Gordon, president of the Canadian National Railways, has turned deaf ears to our appeal to have the basic pension increased. Therefore, the only course left is to appeal to the federal government.
It does appear, having regard to the answer given by the minister, that in fact the officers of the Canadian National Railways in the senior brackets have failed to make the representation on behalf of these discharged veteran employees no longer in the company, and it is necessary that these representations should be made in parliament. Certainly there can be no argument but that they should receive consideration.
I am not going to say more at this time but I do ask, now that the matter has been brought to the attention of the minister- and apparently it was not brought to his attention by the president of the Canadian National Railways-that consideration be given to the representations made by these organizations as well as by the unions. After all, parliament has the final say in matters such as this. I think I understate the case when I say that, as a result of representations made in parliament during a period of years beginning in 1950, consideration was finally given by the Canadian National Railways to the improvement of the general pension system. In no small measure representations made in parliament, where public opinion can be created and where public notice can be brought to injustice, contributed to assuring a reasonable and more effective pension plan having been brought into effect.
My second representation has to do with another matter in connection with Canadian National Railways employees who, as a result of alleged misconduct, are dismissed from the service. These employees have an opportunity of appearing before a representative of the railway company, and they are there asked questions relating to their alleged guilt of the offence with which each, individually, is charged; but they are unable to secure a copy of the particulars of the affidavit or

statutory declaration of evidence upon which the charge against them is based.
I know there have been one or two requests on the part of railway employees to be placed in the position where affidavits will be placed in their hands so they may have the necessary means of establishing that the person or persons who swore or declared the affidavit or declaration, as the case may be, did not tell the truth. I feel it is only justice that a document that represents charges that cause an individual to lose his livelihood should not be denied to the man whose livelihood is lost as a result of a statement made in that affidavit. I am asking the minister to give consideration to having the railway company grant to the individual, whether guilty or not guilty, at least the opportunity of having his day in court if he is permitted to take proceedings against the individual who, under the cloak of anonymity, is able to make charges without being required to appear before the board investigating the matter.
Those are the two matters that I bring to the attention of the minister in connection with railway employees. I congratulate the Canadian National Railways management on what it finally did, after years of procrastination, in bringing into effect a pension plan that is in many ways a model one. It was long delayed, and it will naturally take time for all the anomalies to be ironed out. At the same time, however, there remains a large group of Canadians who are today in receipt of a pitiful pittance of $25 or $30 a month. These men gave the best years of their lives to the service of this country in the national railway system.
Because of the fact these men were discharged at a time when they were unable to make the contributions they should have, or could have otherwise made, they are placed in a position where they are unable to carry on. I join once more with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in pressing in the strongest possible terms the claims of these few thousand people. They will not affect the result of any election campaign. There are a few in each district. There are no votes in this, but there is a real demand for justice on their behalf.

I have spoken on this subject a great many times and on this occasion I had intended to prepare something on our troubles with respect to transportation and the refusal of the different governments to live up to our contract of 1873; and if it had not been so late in the session I would have done so. However, I want to say this. Under the terms of union of 1873, the main reason why we ever joined Canada was that we expected to get transportation. But as all hon. members know, for years we have had difficulties. I blame nearly all governments -but the Liberal government is the greatest often de'r of all the governments-for not giving us a decent deal at all and for not living up to any of the terms of confederation. I might say that from 1873 the different governments tried out different steamers by way of getting transportation to the mainland. Under the Conservative government we obtained a couple of steamers which gave us fairly good transportation facilities in the summer but which were not able to cope with the winter troubles which confronted us in connection with ice.
However, the most trying circumstances and the worst example of all that we had from 1873 to the present time was in 1903. That is 50 years ago. Prior to that time we had had some good crossings and, as I said a moment ago, fair transportation in the summer time. But in the winter of 1903 there was no transportation. Not a pound of freight, not a letter nor a passenger was moved under the government contract for

40 days and 40 nights. I am not blaming the present Minister of Transport on this occasion. I have looked up the records and I find that was apparently the time that he arrived as a resident of Canada by the stork transportation system. However, we will come along later where we can blame him for negligence in not fulfilling-and that quite recently-the demands we have made upon him with reference to transportation.
I am not going to go into details but I want to ask the minister to answer a couple of questions when he is replying. One of them is a question dealing with our trade with Newfoundland. For over 50 years we had with Newfoundland an excellent trade in our farm products. I might say that now is our best opportunity-it is better for Newfoundland and better for Prince Edward Island- because we grow the best food supplies that can be grown anywhere in the world and, if we get the right consideration from the government, they can be easily shipped to the province of Newfoundland.
My question to the minister is this. What kind of service will there be between Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland for this present season? What boat or boats will call, and how often? I might also ask what is the subsidy paid, but I do not care what subsidy is paid because it is a matter of service that is due both to Prince Edward Island and to Newfoundland. This is an extremely important matter to my own province of Prince Edward Island.
I have another item I wish to mention but since I am cutting down on my general resume of hard-luck story with respect to the Liberal party of years past, I am cutting down on that. I want to put on the record another question for the minister to reply to. This system of private enterprise has been operating for some ten years and has been giving wonderful service to the people of Prince Edward Island. With the facilities they offer in the summer season they have certainly helped the Canadian National Railways to fulfil their responsibilities.

The difficulty seems to be that this community is located eight or ten miles from Grand Falls. I suppose the railway management feel that Drummond is located close to a large town and a large railway station, and that therefore it would not be warranted in spending any considerable sum of money at that point. This particular community in the vicinity of Drummond is a farming area, one of the most prosperous in that area served by the northwestern branch of the Canadian National Railways. I believe there is more produce shipped from this area than from any other of its size in that part of New Brunswick.
The people there for some time have been pressing for a proper railway station and way-freight facilities, as well as the facilities afforded by a siding. I visited the community last fall and saw that the railways were enlarging the siding facilities, a fact that was deeply appreciated by the people in the area. Because of the work that has been done on the siding facilities several potato shipping houses will be erected along that line.
The one complaint however is that even yet there is no place to store reefer cars or to have them available. In the last number of years it has been the practice to have reefer cars, when available, placed on track

Supply-Transport
at a point 40 or 50 miles east, near Miramichi. Anyone requiring cars had to wait two or three days for them; and in the winter months they just were not available. This is one area in the province where potato shippers are located, and when potatoes can be shipped it is important that the cars be readily available.
The other point I was about to raise is that at Drummond they have a station-at least, that is how it is described-about the size of a box car. It consists of only two rooms and, I suggest, is not in keeping with the community. The people of that area are not asking for a large station; but I would ask the minister to take note that they do want him to bring to the attention of the proper authorities the fact that they should have a station capable of accommodating those who would use it, and with a full-time clerk or operator in attendance.
At the present time freight is received at that point only in carload lots, but more than two-thirds of the time freight going out must be billed from Grand Falls. This means that the farmer has to drive ten miles to deliver his bill of lading.
The people in that area feel they are not receiving from the C.N.R. the type of service to which they are entitled. I could give several examples where the national railways are losing a considerable amount of business to the C.P.R. I am not sure that the department is interested in securing business for the publicly-owned railways, but I do know of one man who shipped last fall 200 cars of potatoes, but was not given shipping accommodation in the form of a siding in his own community. Perhaps I should do so at this stage, Mr. Chairman, and as briefly as possible. May I first of all thank hon. members, and commend them for the very fair way in which they have criticized the estimates of the Department of Transport. I have listened carefully to the representations made, and I am happy to say to all those members who have spoken that if I am unable to deal with each item specifically I can tell them now that in due course their representations will be considered.
I should like to deal first of all with the statements made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. He repeated in effect this year some of the criticisms he has made against the department, particularly against the maritime commission, and referred to the apparent lack of policy in the maritime commission in so far as deep sea cargo vessels are concerned. Of course he dealt with the whole policy but I have not the time nor do I consider it necessary to deal with that now. ,
I want to say that we have a definite policy in so far as these vessels are concerned. That policy was recommended to us by the Canadian maritime commission. It was a policy that came about following the construction of the Park vessels after the war. My hon. friend will remember that those vessels cost somewhere in the neighbourhood of $277 million and we have recovered practically the whole of that amount. I am not able to say just what amount is still left unrecovered, but it is quite small.
The Canadian maritime commission came into being after that time with Mr. Justice Clyne of the supreme court of British Columbia as chairman. When he was chairman

he recommended to the government the policy that we have tried to follow. That policy, first of all, was to carry out the recommendations that had been made by the government, namely, that the Park vessels should remain under Canadian registry. We tried to make no exception to that, and as a matter of fact there was no exception until the maritime commission, under the chairmanship of Mr. Justice Clyne, recommended the replacement plan.
That plan has worked out very well with one exception, namely deep sea cargo vessels. There is no doubt that in so far as coastal and lake vessels are concerned it has been a success and there is still a substantial amount of money in the fund. But it has not worked out in so far as deep sea vessels are concerned because of the great difference in cost of operating and constructing these vessels as between Canada and the European countries, more particularly the United Kingdom.
Because of that, the maritime commission has had to consider other alternatives. It has had to consider, for instance, the transfer plan which was brought into being at the suggestion of the former chairman and which has had a most beneficial effect. I believe that some 91 ships have been transferred to the United Kingdom by virtue of that plan and there are 55 deep sea vessels now under Canadian registry.
I think that plan saved the day for our merchant marine. In addition the Canadian Vessel Construction Assistance Act was passed under which ship owners and ship operators have benefited substantially. One of the things that the maritime commission has had to consider and is still considering is whether or not it would be advantageous to subsidize these ships. Under the former chairman consideration was given to granting a subsidy of some $25 million or $30 million, but we decided against it because we felt that if we were going to sell our goods to the United Kingdom we should give an opportunity to United Kingdom bottoms to carry the goods that they were purchasing from us. For that and other reasons we determined against a policy of subsidization to that extent.
We have had in existence a committee considering a design for a fast cargo vessel and we are considering ways and means of bringing into being some of these fast ships. But again we are face to face with the same problems we were faced with when Mr. Justice Clyne was chairman of the maritime commission. For instance, the difference in the cost of operating a Canadian flagship and
Supply-Transport
a United Kingdom flagship is $272.50 per day, or approximately $100,000 per annum for each ship. Are we to subsidize the operation of ships to that extent? That would be a very substantial amount of money. We have not determined what we will do but the matter is under active consideration at this time.
My hon. friend inquired as to the number of fast cargo vessels we had under construction. There are two tankers under construction at the Davie shipyard and one bulk freighter. These are for deep sea operation and are the only fast and modern cargo vessels that are under construction at this time.
I could go into other reasons why it is difficult to determine our position at this time. I think I should say that we have received a great deal of advice from ship owners. They have made recommendations to us and are still making recommendations. We are giving those recommendations consideration at this time.
There was the question of the nucleus of men to be employed in both shipping and shipbuilding. I think the number was to be 7,000 employees, but today there are over 19,000 men employed in Canadian shipyards.

I must remind the committee that several years ago the same problem arose and was dealt with by the appointment of a royal commission. Everybody in the house felt that if a royal commission could only be appointed it would move immediately to deal with the various problems affecting freight rates from one end of the country to the other. The royal commission was appointed and everybody complimented that Turgeon commission upon the report which was brought down. We proceeded immediately to put into effect the recommendations of that commission, many of which I am sure have been of great benefit to the various parts of Canada. But I do not think a fair and final judgment on this whole question can be determined until the freight rate equalization policy has been brought to a conclusion. By that I mean the equalization of freight rates which the board of transport commissioners has entered upon, and upon which it held hearings in western Canada in the last three weeks.
A great deal has been said about subsidization. One of the recommendations of the royal commission was a subsidy for the so-called bridge between eastern Canada and western Canada, and that is now in effect. There is in the estimates of the Department of Transport a subsidy of $7 million which provides for the maintenance and operation of the two railways in so far as that is concerned.
Then there are two acts, the Crowsnest rates and the Maritime Freight Rates Act which have not of course been touched or altered in any way by the recommendations of the royal commission; but it may very well be that the equalization judgment or order, which will be brought down by the board of transport commissioners, eventually would have the effect of reducing to some extent at least the rates in so far as the eastern and the western parts of Canada are concerned.
When I hear hon. members say that the government should recast its transportation policy in so far as freight rates are concerned, I would remind them of this. It is the board of transport commissioners, a court of record, that determines the freight rates. Reference is continually made to the railways increasing their rates. It is not the railways that increase their rates; the railways have no authority to increase the general freight rates except by order of the

board. And when there has been an increase it has always been by the board. I am hopeful that the equalization investigation which is now being made by the board will have some beneficial results. I hope that that, together with the recommendations of the royal commission, most of which have been put into effect, will be of benefit. After the equalization order has been brought down, if it is found that it does not meet the position, well, I am sure that the government, whichever government is in office at the time, will be pleased to look at the position to ascertain whether some other remedies cannot be made to meet the situation as it is then found.

I will begin by saying that the matter of increasing the basic pension of $25 per month for retired former employees of the railroad has been considered by the government at various times.
I do not think it was quite fair on the part of the hon. member for Lake Centre to say that the Canadian National Railways had made no representations. I have said in the house that they have recently made no official representations but I must say, in fairness to the officers, that repeatedly the former president of the Canadian National

Supply-Transport
Railways and Mr. Donald Gordon have discussed this matter with me in an informal way in my office; but the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways have not made a formal recommendation to the government in the same manner as they did with reference to the pension fund about which the hon. member for Lake Centre complimented the government. There, of course, I refer to the new revised pension fund. The decision which the government reached was made because it was felt that it would be inconsistent to deal with one group of these pensioners without dealing with the others.
Not very long ago I saw a group of provident fund and Prince Edward Island employees. I think they came to me in December or early January and recommended very strongly in favour of an increase. I gave them the same answer that I had given originally-that until such time as it was possible to deal with all groups, namely, their own groups, the Canadian National Railways employees, superannuated civil servants, pilots and others, it was felt by the government that it would not be right to increase one group without increasing the others.
As of January 1, 1952, there were some 3,223 retired Canadian National Railways employees receiving the basic pension of $25 per month. At July 1, 1952, there were 190 former Canadian government employees in the provident fund receiving the minimum pension of $30 per month. At October 31, 1952, there were 831 retired civil servants receiving pensions of $30 per month-and those people are in a far better position today than they were when my hon. friends brought this problem up originally. That is because today those who are over the age of 70 may apply for the universal old age pension without means test, wherebj' is added $40 per month. Those who are between the ages of 65 and 70 would be entitled to assistance from the provincial government, provided of course that they qualified in regard to means test in accordance with the provisions of the Old Age Assistance Act.
A fact of some importance is that the Canadian National Railways back in 1950 appointed a co-ordinating committee to study and report upon a new pension plan. After careful study, including consultation with representatives of the labour unions, this committee recommended the revised pension plan which became effective on January 1, 1952.
The revised pension plan continues the basic pension of $25 per month payable at the sole expense of the company with the employees having the option of contributing to the pension fund if they desire, and thus
[Mr. Chevrier.l
receiving a larger pension upon retirement. It has been stated that a large number of employees wish to have the basic pension of $25 per month without contributions on their part continued under the new plan. Therefore any increase in the basic pension to presently retired pensioners would appear inconsistent with the provisions of the new plan.
That is the position in a nutshell until it is possible to deal with all these groups, and I hope that will be possible at some future time.

I see my hon. friend from Queens looking at me with great attention and perhaps I should go on to his question. It is subsidized by the province and therefore the Department of Transport has no jurisdiction over it-so I would suggest that he direct his questions to the provincial governments.

I think that is all I should say at this time.

I should like to have the indulgence of the committee for a few

I claim that it is most inadequate. I hope the minister is somewhat familiar with our maritime provinces fisheries. If he is familiar with the system we have in the province of New Brunswick and in the other maritime provinces with respect to our fisheries, which is one of our major industries, he will at once realize that buoys are extremely important.
May I say to the minister that buoys are just like eyes to the fishermen. In our harbours, dredging, lighthouses and beacon lights are important. I submit that buoys are also important. I heard of an old sea captain once saying to his crew-and this was in the days of the old sailing schooners-that if you have lots of water under your keel and you know where you are going, you are all right.
I suggest that in the county of Gloucester there is, on the part of the officials of the minister's department, inadequate attention to the maintenance of our buoy service. There are certain important harbours in Gloucester county as far as our fishing fleet is concerned. May I mention particularly the entrance to Shippigan gully, Shippigan harbour, Lameque harbour and Caraquet harbour. I do not have any details as to the three first mentioned but with respect to Caraquet harbour I possess details which I should like to bring to the attention of the minister this afternoon.
On February 13, 1953, I wrote a letter to the director of marine services of the minister's department asking for improvements in the system of buoys marking the entrance channel to Caraquet harbour. On February 23 I received a reply from the director of marine services, and I wish to quote one paragraph from this letter. It reads as follows:
Caraquet entrance channel is now marked by a good set of range lights and the buoys are installed to augment the range system. This service is also handled by a contractor and consequently the size of the buoys used is limited by the equipment available to the contractors. The matter of improving the buoy system is being looked into.
May I stress this sentence:
This service is also handled by a contractor and consequently the size of the buoys used is limited by the equipment available to the contractor.
I submit that this is a false position to be assumed by the officials of the minister's department because, as I intend to prove, if the system of buoys at the entrance to Caraquet harbour is not adequate, we should not
Supply-Transport
be penalized. Our fishing fleet should not be exposed for the simple reason that the contractor who has the contract for the maintenance of these buoys is not properly equipped to handle large buoys.

Having received this specific information, I conveyed it to the director of marine services of the Department of Transport by a letter of April 21, 1953, to which I have not yet received a reply. I therefore request the permission of this committee to cite the suggestion which I was making to the director of marine services in this letter, and which is as follows:
They-
The pilots.
-suggest that the first buoy at the entrance of the Caraquet harbour, sailing from Shippigan, should be one nine feet and one half lighted (9i') bell buoy.
The three next buoys in the Caraquet harbour should be six feet lighted buoys and they also ask for two similar gas-lighted buoys for the channel on the westerly side of the Caraquet islands.
Summarizing their request and in accordance with the information I have already received from your division the pilots therefore recommend:
(1)	One BWVS No. 18-6, 9J' lighted bell buoy.

As I have just remarked, I have yet received no answer from the director of marine services. It may be that I shall have to wait because the matter might be under investigation by the officials.
