Item agreed to.
131. Departmental administration, $298,800.

Mr. Chairman, on January 28 we had a full day of debate concerning fisheries, in consequence of a resolution in the name of the hon. member for Charlotte. At that time I had only one minute in which to speak at the close of the debate, and I promised that when the estimates for this department were called I would answer on this general administration item the questions then asked.
The hon. members for Charlotte, Gloucester, Halifax, Saint John-Albert, Burin-Burgeo, Iles-de-la-Madeleine, St. John's West, Digby-Yarmouth and Grand Falls-White Bay all asked that some form of fishermen's insurance be instituted to cover boats and gear. I am happy to announce that the government has decided to inaugurate such a scheme. I shall give the details when the appropriate item, No. 766, is before the committee.
The hon. member for Charlotte spoke about the price spread between the prices paid to fishermen and the prices paid by housewives who buy fish in this country. Our department is quite conscious of the problem. Today a fisherman on the east coast gets about 3J cents for cod, and the final price up here in Ottawa is between 40 and 50 cents, ft takes three pounds of cod to make one pound of fillets, so that raises the price to about 10J cents. Processing on the east coast brings the price up to about 17 cents when the fillets leave the east coast. There is a very large spread between the 17 cents paid there and the 40 cents paid up here. I have asked our marketing division to begin a preliminary investigation to see where that spread is.
Fish, of course, is a very perishable product. There is undoubtedly considerable loss from spoilage in transit, and when it is being held. Also the volume of sales is rather erratic, because much of the fish is sold on only one day in the week.
The hon. member for Gloucester raised one or two problems. He asked what steps we were taking to stop the passage of a bill before the Massachusetts legislature requiring the pasteurization of canned lobster. Of course there is very little our government can do to prevent the passage of a bill through that state legislature, just as there is very little a member of that legislature

could do to stop a private member's bill going through this house. The bill has not been passed, and if it should pass we would have to review the situation. Boston is one of the main markets for our lobster, and we would have to do what we could.
The hon. member spoke about the need for dredging the Shippigan gully. Our inspectors report that there is a real need there, and I have asked my colleague, the Minister of Public Works, to try to do some of that dredging this summer.
The hon. member for Selkirk, one of the few prairie members who spoke, asked that some aid be given toward co-operative education to be carried out in one of the prairie universities so that prairie fishermen could have the benefit of these courses. We give assistance to only three universities, St. Francis Xavier in Nova Scotia, Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere in Quebec and British Columbia university. Assistance is given where courses are already provided by the university. I am sure that if a prairie university were to inaugurate such courses we would give sympathetic consideration to making a grant. I might say that the problem in Newfoundland is now before us because the new university down there is obviously a good location for such courses in co-operative education.
The hon. members for Burin-Burgeo and Iles-de-la-Madeleine both spoke of the need for further exploratory services in the gulf of St. Lawrence to locate the large schools of herring which are known to be there but which are difficult for the fishing fleets in operation to locate. We will extend this exploratory work this summer.
The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo also asked that additional protective services be provided on the salmon streams in Labrador. Up until recently there was not great need for such protective services because those streams were not fished extensively by sports fishermen. However, with the establishment of air bases there and with the iron ore development just over the boundary there has been considerable fishing of these streams, and this summer we are substantially increasing the number of guardians.
Both hon. members asked that the provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act be widened to provide unemployment insurance for fishermen. We have had a report on this suggestion from the unemployment insurance commission. It is shown that under the act as passed by this parliament it would be very difficult to include any selfemployed group such as farmers, fishermen or small businessmen. The act provides for
Supply-Fisheries
contributions by the employer, the employee and the government. The relationship between the work and the worker is such that he becomes unemployed involuntarily, not through a decision of his own. Fishermen and farmers are scarcely in that category. At various times consideration has been given to extending the coverage to them, but it certainly could not be done within our present unemployment insurance act.
There are one or two countries in Europe which have fishermen's funds, but they are more in the nature of relief funds. They are raised by a levy on every pound of fish that is caught. Of course it is easier to do that in a country where you have a single agency handling all fish, and it would be much more difficult in this country. We are going to look further into the matter this year.
This year we have a new form of insurance for fishermen's boats and one type of gear. With the experience we gather in the first year or two of the operation of this scheme we may be able to widen it out into some form of unemployment insurance for fishermen.
The hon. member for Digby-Yarmouth and the hon. member for Nanaimo both raised the matter of extending the limit of Canadian territorial waters. This subject was discussed at considerable length in the fisheries committee this year, and subsequent to that there was a debate in this house when the two international conventions were being considered. I have nothing to add to these debates.
The hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay asked what we were going to do in connection with the development of Labrador fishing. Since that time we have had the Walsh report on the development in Newfoundland generally, and in the estimates there is provision for the commencement of such a program. I shall speak of it later when the particular item is up.
Finally, the hon. member for Norfolk asked what progress we were making in obtaining an international great lakes fisheries treaty of the type that has worked so well on the west coast. This would provide necessary research for the fisheries of the great lakes and also control of the scourge of lamprey eels which has so greatly reduced the commercial catch of fish in the great lakes.
We were hopeful that we could have had such a treaty with the United States, but we ran into a little difficulty this spring. Here in Canada the primary control of fishing rests with the federal government. The province of Ontario actually manage their own fisheries, but there is the most harmonious

Supply-Fisheries
relationship between the two departments, so there has been no trouble on this side. In the United States the control of the fisheries rests primarily with the states and there are nine states involved in the great lakes fisheries. There was a little difficulty in reconciling their points of view, so we were unable to conclude such a treaty this year.
However, there has been a decision on both sides of the boundary to go ahead with separate programs. In the estimates there is an item of $50,000 to undertake lamprey control up at Sault Ste. Marie where the lampreys are coming into lake Superior, and an item of $10,000 for research generally in connection with great lakes fisheries. The province of Ontario is matching that $10,000 so there will be $20,000 available for biological research in connection with the fisheries of the great lakes.

I am interested to hear that the government intends to provide an insurance scheme for fishermen's gear and boats. In view of the fact that in Quebec the fisheries are under the control of the provincial government, will this insurance extend to that province?
I think it would be better to deal with that matter under the actual item, which is item 766.

My first words will be of congratulation to the Minister of Fisheries on behalf of my constituents for having decided at long last to bring in a scheme of insurance to cover fishermen's boats and gear. I have only been in this house a short time but I have long realized the necessity for such a scheme of insurance. Along with other hon. members of this house who are interested in fisheries, I have taken advantage of every opportunity to bring this matter to the attention of the officials of the Department of Fisheries. On behalf of my constituents I want to thank the minister for the most commendable scheme which is being set up. I shall be interested in hearing the details later.
On March 26 last I filed a notice of inquiry of the Department of Fisheries with reference to the then dangerous position of the fresh fillet markets. My questions were as follows:
1.	Has the Department of Fisheries any information on the large quantities of fillets from last year's maritime provinces' catch still in storage unsold or still held on the American market?
2.	Has the Department of Fisheries been informed of a substantial reduction in the price of cod, during the coming fishing season, consequent upon the losses sustained by maritime provinces' packers of fillets on last year's catch?
3.	Has the said department under advisement any plan to set a reasonable floor price for maritime provinces' codfish for the 1953 season or some other system of assisting or subsidizing the cod fishing industry?
IMr. Sinclair.]
In answer to this inquiry I was advised almost immediately, through the generosity and quick attention of the parliamentary assistant, that as of March 1, 1953, there were
3.915.000	pounds of fresh frozen Atlantic cod fillets held in Canada as compared with
942.000	pounds on March 1, 1952, besides the stocks of Canadian fish held in the United States. This in itself was a most embarrassing situation, as you may realize, for our fish processors. I was also advised at that time that the price of cod to the fishermen for the 1953 summer season had not yet been established, and that the fisheries prices support board were keeping very close watch on the current situation and would be prepared to make recommendations to the government should conditions warrant such action when the new price levels would be established.
I have lately been informed, Mr. Chairman, that the prices-they may not be definitely settled-now mentioned by northern New Brunswick fish merchants for cod and flounders are as follows: For cod of 2J pounds and up, 2 cents per pound; for cod between 1 and 1J pounds and up to 2\ pounds in weight, 1 cent per pound. Compare these prices with the average price of cod last year -and last year there was no distinction between small and large cod-of 2| cents per pound. The minister will realize that this is quite a substantial difference. Last year flounders commanded a price of between 2f and 3 cents per pound; the price being offered now is 1J cents a pound. I am further informed-and I know this information is correct because I happen to know a little about codfish-that it costs our cod fishermen If cents a pound to get their catch and bring it to the wharf or the harbour where it is marketed. Therefore one may immediately realize that with that price now fixed or offered, our fishermen are bound to suffer very heavy losses in the course of the next season. As a matter of fact, they will not be able to carry on any fishing operations.
I am also informed, although from unofficial sources, that the market within the last week looks better for the cod fishermen. I hope that is correct. If not, if there is no substantial betterment in cod marketing conditions, then I would suggest to the minister that the necessary steps be taken to provide some assistance through the Fisheries Prices Support Act to maintain our most important codfish industry at a reasonable paying level for our cod fishermen.
I would also point out to the minister that I have received several communications from smaller operators, smaller cod processors and

merchants within the last few months, advising me that owing to the enormous losses they have suffered on account of the falling market for fresh cod and sole fillets last year they will be unable to go back into business this year. When one considers that our fish merchants have lost as much as 6 cents a pound on fillets owing to falling markets in the United States, then I think it is easily understandable that the smaller merchants certainly cannot continue doing business, which would be most unfortunate.
On the other hand I am advised, and I think quite officially, that there is absolutely no system under which the fish merchants can be assisted by way of loans or subsidies.
I submit that this should be taken into very serious consideration by the minister with a view to setting up some system, plan or scheme whereby our fish merchants, who are hit hard by a falling market, may be protected in order that our industry can survive.
I do not wish to speak at any great length tonight on fisheries, although I have lots to say. I realize that the time is short and the minister is very anxious to pass his estimates. I shall make one more observation before resuming my seat concerning our oyster fisheries in the county of Gloucester.
I was rather surprised to learn, in answer to a question which I put on the order paper, that in my county alone we have 420 oyster leases of oyster farms as against six for the county of Westmorland, and these are the only 426 oyster farms or leases under federal jurisdiction in the whole of the province of New Brunswick. I will not say that I am somewhat prejudiced when I am speaking about oysters; but I happen to own an oyster farm myself in the district of Shippigan, and therefore I believe I know a little about oyster culture.
I am going to suggest to the minister-and again may I say I am doing this not as an oyster farmer but on behalf of those who are interested in oyster culture in my county of Gloucester-that the rentals collected for the oyster leases by the Department of Fisheries should be done away with altogether. In my submission they are nothing but a nuisance tax, because after all it is nothing but a nominal fee that the owners of the oyster leases have to pay every year. As a matter of fact, last year in the three provinces of Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick the total collected in rentals for oyster leases by the Department of Fisheries was only $1,818.58. In my county of Gloucester in the province of New Brunswick we paid $331.50 for oyster leases as
Supply-Fisheries
against $19 for the county of Westmorland.
I submit that this nominal fee should be abolished.
Although I did ask a question as to what it cost the department to collect these small licence fees, I could not be informed of this for the simple reason that the department said it was not possible to segregate this particular cost from the other costs of administration. My submission to the minister is that it must cost as much, if not more, to collect these nominal rentals for leases, than it brings in, and that as a matter of fact it should be done away with.
As I said before, Mr. Chairman, I could say much more on fisheries. But before resuming my seat, I should be remiss in my duty if I did not again thank the minister on behalf of my constituents and the fishermen of Gloucester county for the very good news that he has announced to the house tonight by telling us that a scheme or plan of fishermen's insurance to cover boats and gear will soon be initiated by his department.

I shall also be brief in my remarks because I, too, realize that the minister is most anxious to get his estimates through as soon as possible, and I imagine other cabinet ministers are also anxious to get finished as soon as possible. But I do want to congratulate the minister on the announcement he has made tonight. It is something that members representing fishing constituencies have discussed and asked for, for a long time. I do believe it is a step in the right direction, and even though at the beginning it may seem to be of minor importance-it will take time to take into consideration all the different branches of the industry which may need some sort of protection-it is a step in the right direction.
I believe the minister and the officials of his department are to be congratulated, because I fully realize the enormous amount of research that is required in connection with this insurance plan. Since it is something new it will take a great deal of study, and those who are responsible for bringing in this great improvement certainly deserve all the credit.
I want to congratulate the minister and say that although he has been with the department only a short time he has made a very fine impression on the industry in all parts of Canada. I say that in all sincerity. In the past it has appeared to me in too many instances that the fisheries department was considered to be a minor department. I had hoped that we might have a minister who would stick with the department and try to

Supply-Fisheries
do the things that fishermen feel should be done. In the eight years I have been here in Ottawa we have had five or six different ministers. The late Hon. Frank Bridges, a young man from my own province, had ideas and vision, and would have done a lot for the fishermen of this country but unfortunately two years after he took over the department he died. That was a great loss to my province and to the whole country. Today we have had a young man take over this department and, in the short time he has been there, I can see that there has been great improvement. I have every hope and belief that we may expect those improvements to continue in the future.
As I said, Mr. Chairman, my remarks will be brief, but I also wish to congratulate the minister and his officials on the demonstrations they have put on in the west block with the competent cooks they have in their department. They have endeavoured to show members here on parliament hill, their wives, and some outsiders that fish when properly cooked is the best food in the world. Those of us who come from down by the salt water realize that. The demonstrations have been a great help and a great credit to the department. I only wish we could have more of them in different parts of Canada to show people how fish should be cooked. I was fortunate in being asked over to a luncheon about a month ago and 25 or 30 members of parliament had a most enjoyable meal. I can assure you that those responsible for putting on that dinner knew how to cook fish. If more was done along the line of educating the people how to cook fish I am sure it would be a great benefit to the industry.
There is just one other matter I wish to mention briefly and I believe it means more to the fishermen of the maritime provinces than anything that has been done by this department in a long, long time. I refer to the very friendly and co-operative spirit that has been developed in recent months between the fisheries department in the United States and the fisheries department here in Canada.
I believe that is one thing for which the minister deserves a lot of credit. We who live in the Atlantic provinces realize that without United States markets our fishing industry would be at a pretty low ebb. Prices are pretty well established by those prevailing in the United States. In order to take advantage of that market we have to deal with people outside our country, but in the past there has been little co-operation between the fisheries department here and the fisheries department in the United States.
I believe this has been one of the major accomplishments of the Minister of Fisheries

since he has taken office. I wish him every success in this line and I trust he will continue his efforts to develop that friendship which means so much to fishermen on the Atlantic coast. I hope the minister knows from his own experience in the industry, as I can tell him from my personal knowledge that without those markets in the United States we who depend on the industry for a livelihood would have been pretty disappointed many years ago.
I might also add in that connection that there has been set up in that section recently a sardine fishermen's organization. When it was being discussed I suggested that it would be impossible for it to function properly unless it was developed internationally. In other words, if prices of sardines are set here in Canada-and this applies to any other fish-because we have to depend on export markets it would be almost impossible for us to establish those prices without the co-operation of canners in the United States. I hope the department will go a long way toward developing greater co-operation, because I believe the fishermen of the United States realize that they have the same problems we have here on this side of the border. I believe that co-operation by both sides can do a lot for the fishing industry.
Before I resume my seat I want to say a word in connection with the sardine industry and I shall be through. During the past year, 1952, our sardine fishermen had a most discouraging season. Prices dropped from $20 per hogshead to $6 or $7 in the summer months when the supply was plentiful, and when the fishermen might have made a good season's pay. However, shortly after the price dropped the catch dropped. During the winter, although purse seiners crossed the bay of Fundy every day that it was fit to be on the water, they were unable to find any winter sardines. The result was that this spring canners were left with no stocks on Hand at all. The price is back to $20 at the present time due to scarcity. I believe that the sardine fishermen in the 'Quoddy area may look forward to a very good season if the catch improves, as we have every reason to believe it will.
Again I want to congratulate the minister on the good word he has brought to us tonight. I can assure him that it will be received most enthusiastically by fishermen on the Atlantic coast. He has been doing a fine job, I know he is going to continue to do a fine job, and that he is going to stay with this department and give us a hand.

Mr. Chairman, I am going to be as brief as possible, but there is some information I would like.

First of all I would like also to pay tribute to the minister in the work he is trying to do. He is really taking an interest in his job, and I think he is making some progress. However, as the deputy minister has pointed out on many occasions, the main problem in the fishing industry is marketing. If the department works as hard as it has been doing for the last year it should show considerable improvement but, again as the deputy minister has said on many occasions, the marketing of fish in Canada today is a job. Not only are you pushing fish on the market, you are replacing some other attractive commodity, and that is difficult. We recognize that situation and I know that most members of the house, particularly those who are members of the fisheries committee, have been willing to do what they could in order to make the problem known.
I think charity begins at home in the matter of marketing and we have a restaurant in this building which turns out very poor fish. I too had that meal over in the west block kitchen, and it was an excellent meal. It showed that properly cooked fish can compete with anything that goes on a table. I trust that after the next election when we get back here-whoever gets back-a restaurant committee will be set up in this House of Commons which will take more interest in the restaurant and cafeteria than has been shown in the past.
I think one of the first things the minister should do is to get the ladies he has over in that kitchen, bring them up to this restaurant and instruct the chef and others concerned in how to prepare a proper meal of fish. There is no point in talking about selling that fish a thousand miles away from here. We should make a start right here. One of the best places in Canada to advertise would be by putting up two meals a week as a demonstration to those who use that dining-room that fish can compete with any other commodity that goes on the table.
Before the minister's estimates are concluded I want him to tell me just what place the fisheries prices support appropriation has played in the life of the fishing industry. A moment ago he mentioned that the price the fishermen received for fish on the east coast is ridiculous. I have had correspondence with the department recently, and 1 know that the deputy minister is familiar with the point I am going to mention. For the record, I should like the minister to give me an explanation as to why this sort of thing should exist. I have in my hand a letter that is dated April 28. It is from a fisherman in the Louisburg area in which there is a
Supply-Fisheries
large fishing plant owned by the Gorton-Pew Company.
This correspondence says something about prices. The minister indicated what one has to pay for fish in central Canada, somewhere around 40 to 45 cents a pound. Here is the story of the fisherman who catches the fish. He says:
As of April 25 for 5,000 pounds of fish the fishermen received $100 from Gorton-Pew; of this $100 $20 would cover boat loan and boat upkeep, $17 would go for 200 pound squid bait at 85 cents per pound, $16 for 400 pound herring bait at 4 cents, $10 for food for four men, $22 for baiting trawl and $16.40 for 60 gallons of gas. That's a total of $101.40, and no allowance for oil, hooks, or return on their investment, nor loss of trawl, a string of which costs approximately $6. In other words, in order to make $100 a catch must be well over 25 tons of fish.
He is practically in debt when he finishes up, but he has had the pleasure of fishing. I continue quoting the letter:
For the week ending April 25 a boat with a four-man crew caught 12,000 pounds of fish in two sets which extended over a period of 20 hours each. For their 40 hours of labour each man received $23.41.
Now, he poses this question:
Why does the government permit an American company to come in here and pay 2 cents to Canadian fishermen while the Canadian company at the plant pays 25 cents and 3 cents. In fact we are told our Liberal government helped this American company get established here.
He mentions mechanization, and the rest of the letter is irrelevant. The point I wanted to bring out was the amount received by the man who actually caught the fish, and the spread between what that person received for his labour and the amount the consumer had to pay for fish. There is a terrific spread, and I think there is room for an investigation by the department into why that spread should exist.
The point upon which I should like to focus the minister's attention is the price of bait. These bait freezing plants are subsidized quite heavily by the government, sometimes by both the federal and provincial governments. 1 am not singling out the Gorton-Pew Company as being bad, but that letter would indicate that they discriminate against this particular type of fisherman. Unless you can get bait, you cannot fish. The price was 8J cents a pound for squid bait and 4 cents a pound for ordinary bait. I think that price is out of line in view of the fact that most of the money that goes into the establishment of these bait freezing plants is government money. I am asking the minister-I know he will do this-to check on that particular complaint from that

Supply-Fisheries
area-to ascertain whether or not the fishermen there are getting a square deal from this company.
I would be obliged if the minister would tell me just what place the fisheries prices support legislation has played in connection with seeing that at least reasonable prices are maintained for the man who actually catches the fish. In effect, the fisherman is in the hands of the company from whom he buys this bait. If he does not market through a company of that size he does not get any bait and he cannot market his fish anywhere else.
I should like to leave this thought with the minister. The grain industry in this country had a rather rough road to travel before we had the international wheat agreement. Before we had a board whose job it was to manage the industry, market the wheat and conduct negotiations with the rest of the grain producing countries in the world with a view to getting an international agreement, the industry had a difficult time. I believe the fish industry of this country is rapidly approaching the time when we are going to need some kind of machinery within the department that will have the right to probe world markets, and be able to do the kind of job for the fishing industry that the wheat board is doing for the grain industry.
If the minister has any information on those points, I shall appreciate it.

I should like to join with hon. members who have already spoken, the hon. member for Gloucester and others, with reference to the pleasant announcement made by the minister. For over a year now we have been battling to get some form of insurance or protection for the fishermen in our different constituencies. As the other speakers have said, this announcement will be received with great rejoicing by all the fishermen in my locality.
There is a matter which I mentioned last year, and which I think comes directly under this item of departmental administration. There was a heavy storm on the Atlantic coast during which a ship called the Winnie Anne was lost. I want to deal with that question because it is now up to the Department of Fisheries to look into it. Last year I spoke about the poor coastal service protection for seamen and others, which was brought out by the loss of this vessel. I think it was the firm of Sweeney and Company or Sweeney Brothers who launched the boats in that desperate storm and really saved the crew of the Winnie Anne. I hope they have been 
recompensed for that act of bravery and hardship.
There is no doubt that the men in the department as well as the minister and the parliamentary assistant know the details in connection with this matter. I am informed that the insurance people have issued a cheque in full to the owner of the Winnie Anne and that that cheque is still in his possession, unless it has been forced away from him within the last two or three weeks. He has not been recompensed at all. For instance, we know that the Winnie Anne was subsidized to a certain extent. But at the same time, why was this matter not settled? If it is settled now, that is what I want to know. If the owner has received his proper allotment out of it, I am sure there is no need of my arguing the case any further. If I get a nod from anybody over there on the other side indicating that it is settled, I shall not say any more. Apparently it is not settled yet. Then I shall have to talk on.
What I want to know is this. Why is this man held up on a transaction of this kind? He has done practically everything that it is possible for a man to do. He held the cheque. He should never have surrendered that cheque because, as I understand it, it was made out in his name. If the crown were so anxious to get back their share of the subsidy, then the balance of it should have been sent to the treasury board and the treasury board should have authorized the Minister of Fisheries to place in the estimates here an amount with which to pay the owner of the Winnie Anne. I shall rest my case right there for the moment and wait till I find out what the situation is. I know the minister is anxious to say something in regard to this matter.

Mr. Chairman, the subject matter of fisheries is a most important one and merits a much longer debate than it will receive on this occasion. I think we all realize that the minister is anxious to get his estimates through, and that the house is anxious to conclude its business. One therefore must speak briefly on matters which warrant much more attention.
In the first place, I want to join with the others in their references to this insurance fund. We have not the details of it yet but we will get them in a little while. I think any further remarks should be deferred until after we get them.
I also want to associate myself in some respects with the remarks made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South. Certainly the problem of the marketing of fish today is a most serious one. The fishing industry is facing a depressed condition, if not a depres-

sion. There is, I think, a feeling of pessimism permeating the entire industry. I realize that it is not an easy matter with which to deal, but I believe that more attention should be paid to this problem of marketing than has been paid to it heretofore.
I rise particularly, Mr. Chairman, to draw the attention of the minister to a matter with which I know he is somewhat conversant and about which he has heard before, namely the problem of trawlers operating in our coastal waters. When the minister was in Halifax a short time ago I believe he made one or two trips down the eastern shore or perhaps the western shore of Halifax and met with some fishermen there. Certainly when I was in Halifax some four weeks ago, I happened to meet a group of 18 or 20 of them from the St. Margaret bay area, all of whom were tremendously concerned over this matter. The same situation applies, I think, with respect to coastal fishermen generally. Certainly it does to the fishermen in my constituency along the bay of Fundy.
The problem is an easy one to explain. We have this situation. Our own Canadian trawlers, financed by Canadian money and manned by Canadian crews are, by their licences, kept outside of the 12-mile limit, and they cannot come within that limit and operate. However, the United States trawlers are, by international law, shall we say, permitted to come within three miles of our coast line. The result is that those trawlers are operating again this year in larger numbers than heretofore. They are somewhat cyclical; like birds of various kinds, they come and they go. Three or four years ago they were here in large numbers, and they are back again.
With the United States trawlers operating up to and, I may say, sometimes well within the three-mile limit, the result is that our small draggers are operating right up against our coast line and the hand-line fishermen have been driven ashore. That is the position as they see it. Their whole way of life is threatened. Their gear is being damaged and they believe the fishing grounds are being destroyed. They have real cause for concern.
What can we do about it? I know that if one suggests doing anything in so far as United States trawlers are concerned the suggestion is immediately made: "Are you willing to jeopardize your position and lose the United States market for that fish?" Naturally one does not want to do that. However, Mr. Chairman, I am sure the United States fishery officers, the officers of the
Supply-Fisheries
United States government, are reasonable men.
A few moments ago we heard the hon. member for Charlotte commending the minister with regard to the most friendly relations which now exist between the United States department and our own. If the officers and representatives of that department of the United States government sat around the table with our own minister and representatives of our department, and if it was explained to the Americans-something they will know anyway-that our fishermen are prohibited from operating within the 12-mile limit, and if they were asked for co-operation -with no waving of a club, no shaking of the fist and no making of threats-I cannot help believing that as reasonable men they would be willing to come to some modus vivendi whereby at least a greater degree of co-operation could be achieved than that which is now in evidence. I am quite certain that if this matter were put to them in the right way an agreement could be reached whereby United States trawlers would stay outside the 12-mile limit, or at least some reasonable distance. That would give our small draggers a chance to operate farther away from the coast. It would preserve the inshore fishing waters for our coastal fishermen.
They have achieved a way of life along that coast of ours in Nova Scotia, in these little communities on these bays and inlets. They have never made a great deal of money, but they have achieved a manner of living which they enjoy. They have achieved independence. They have maintained their homes there for generations. Many of these places were established two centuries ago. If present conditions are allowed to continue, the existence of these communities will be threatened, and I believe the communities themselves may be destroyed. The matter does not involve a tremendous number of people.
I realize that one cannot stand in the way of progress. In so far as deep sea fishing is concerned, I realize that the trawler is here to stay and must be recognized. We realize that the quarrels and dissensions of 20 years ago are now things of the past. But when you come to these coastal waters and to these communities, I say some steps should be taken to preserve their industry and their way of life; and I believe something can be done. As the hon. member for Charlotte said, we have a new minister who has shown energy and imagination in dealing with problems. I ask him to give to this problem his special attention and consideration. If he

Supply-Fisheries
does so, I believe something can be done which will help. That is all I have to say.

Mr. Chairman, like other hon. members I was very pleased to hear the announcement made by the Minister of Fisheries this evening that he proposed to give us details regarding the scheme of insurance against storm damage to gear and equipment of fishermen. This is a subject upon which a good many members have spoken, and concerning which there have been expressions of opinion in many newspapers in maritime fishing areas.
However, I am sure the minister and hon. members generally will be interested to learn that in the latest newspaper I have received from St. John's the premier of Newfoundland made a pronouncement on this same subject which is exactly contrary to that made tonight by the minister. In this newspaper article the premier said he had been trying for a long time to get a scheme of insurance, that he had even raised the question with Lloyd's but that he had been turned down. Then he said this:
Over half a million dollars was held in the treasury in trust for the fishermen, and the government was anxious to find some way in which it could be applied for the benefit of all the fishing population, to whom it belonged.
He recalled that the government at an earlier session proposed a fishermen's insurance act. which was outlined in a curricular letter, and the opinion of the fishing population sought. The fishermen turned it down, and the government dropped the idea.
Unfortunately, the approach to Lloyd's was not successful either, sinc^it was found that to insure such a vast amount of property against storm damage in a region where storms are so frequent, half a million dollars would be only a drop in the bucket. So the government still had the half million and was still looking for something to do with it.
The minister has accomplished something which our very active premier has been unable to do, and accordingly deserves congratulations.
In the course of his very brief remarks- and I regret they were so brief-the minister failed to make any reference to the great

report which we have had from the joint development committee. He did refer to co-operative education, one of the minor recommendations in the report, but the subject, probably, upon which the whole report should be based.
I have had the pleasure of a long acquaintance with the co-operative movement as it has developed at St. Francis Xavier, and I would like to say that the co-operative educational system has to begin from the bottom and work up. It is not something that can be imposed from the top. It is a slow and gradual process, based upon educational methods applied to adults. In fact it is not called a co-operative movement at St. Francis Xavier so much as it is called adult education for co-operative action.
I must make some reference to the Walsh report, and I hope the minister will find opportunity to do so, too. This committee, called the joint development committee, was one of the two appointed by the federal government, one in Prince Edward Island and the other in Newfoundland. The committee appointed in Newfoundland consisted of officials of the provincial department of fisheries and the federal Department of Fisheries, with the chief justice of Newfoundland as chairman. It sat two years, patiently gathering and sifting the evidence, and getting large numbers of reports on different aspects of the fisheries. Now it has made its report, a copy of which was given to me by the minister some time ago. After two years of working on such a subject I would hope to hear from the minister officially this evening as to what he thinks about the recommendations.
After a body as skilled as this one has considered a subject for two years, he would be a rash man indeed who would rush in without adequate consideration and attempt to criticize. I have no intention of doing so tonight, and shall not until I have been able to digest it and discuss it with fishing representatives in my constituency. Until that time I do not feel competent to express any criticism with respect to it.
I would point out, however, that it recommends very radical changes in the fishing industry. The fishing industry has been highly individualized in Newfoundland until very recently, and all the fishermen have had little establishments of their own. I do not mean that each fisherman conducts his own establishment, but there would be small groups with their own outfits, their own vessel, fishing gear, nets, hooks, lines and the other necessary equipment. They would obtain supplies for that vessel and engage a
Supply-Fisheries
crew of three, four or five men. Then other groups of men would stay on shore where they would have an establishment consisting of a storehouse, stages, motorboats, nets, twine, lines, anchors and all the rest of the equipment. Men working together in groups of four, five, six or sometimes ten or twelve have carried on the fishing industry for centuries.
As far as I can understand this report the principal recommendation is that there should be established central curing depots which would be supplied with fish caught by trawlers or draggers, in comparison with the type of boat now used by the ordinary fisherman. There would be a continual supply of different varieties of fish. The fisherman would not be concerned merely with catching codfish; he would catch flounders which formerly were thrown overboard, rosefish, haddock and other varieties. The emphasis would be laid upon fresh fillets about which we heard such a sad story tonight from the hon. member for Gloucester.
Hon. members may remember that on many occasions I have spoken in this house about the traditional markets that existed in Spain, Portugal and other European countries as well as in Brazil. An article which appeared in the Daily News referred to those past days when we supplied Spain with about 400,000 quintals of salt codfish, Portugal with as much as 300,000 quintals every year, and Brazil took as much as 200,000 quintals. In other words, more than 75 per cent of the catch of over one million quintals would be disposed of to those three countries. Then Italy and Greece would buy large quantities of salt codfish.
But what is the situation today? Those markets have gone, and for years hardly a codfish has been sold to Brazil. We had to ask the Portuguese government to buy some of our codfish this year. We had to ask the Spanish government to do it last year. It seems to me extremely regrettable that these large markets have been allowed to go to pieces. I cannot understand how the men interested in the fishing industry of Newfoundland could have allowed those markets to decline so rapidly without making a terrific effort to save them.
I believe it was because of the fantastic interest that has developed in the fresh fish market in the United States, with its quick turnover. The processing plants were able to deal quickly with the fish they bought from the fishermen and which could be sold in the United States. It is not a good thing to have all your eggs in one basket, and I have said here on several occasions that it was a bad thing for us to depend too much

Supply-Fisheries
on the fresh fish market in the United States.
Despite what the hon. member for Charlotte said here tonight, despite the good will that may exist between the fisheries department in Washington and the Department of Fisheries in Ottawa, there is still the danger that representations may be made by fishing interests there which would hamper the sale of our fish in the United States market. No doubt there is a large market in a country with 160 million people, but as the Minister of Fisheries pointed out this evening, as you leave the coast the cost goes up because of various factors, the chief of which is transportation.
It is a strange thing that in the report by the commission in 1927 all the commissioners except the chairman advised against the use of trawlers. Today we have come to the position where trawlers or some kind of vessel using drag nets or seines are recommended as the best method of prosecuting this industry.
I know hon. members are impatient and anxious to let the minister get ahead with his estimates, but I feel I should emphasize this phase of the voluminous report made by the committee in Newfoundland; that is, the importance of having a sound system of co-operative education available to the fishermen before any extensive or radical changes are made in the method of fishing.
There is one feature that sticks in my mind, the suggestion that the fishermen will be able to purchase shares in the companies that will operate these central curing establishments. I do not know how that is going to work out. It does not seem to me to be in the realm of practical business, but I do hope it will be possible for the fishermen to buy the establishments to which they will sell their fish. I have no doubt that the minister has given serious consideration to this report, and when we get on the items he will be able to say what he is going to do this year. I know he will not be able to do very much, but he should make a beginning. I see signs in the estimates of that. I shall defer any further comments until we get to the various items.

Mr. Chairman, I feel I should answer the points that have been raised by various hon. members. The hon. member for Gloucester and the hon. member for Cape Breton South referred to prices support on the east coast markets for fresh fillets. It is quite true that a difficult situation arose in the United States market, mainly due to the influx of great quantities of Icelandic fillets which had been cut out of the British

market. The situation is improving, as the stocks are now down to 8,000,000 pounds. Fortunately our Canadian plants have low inventories.
The fisheries prices support board met in the maritimes last month and discussed the situation with both the fishermen and the fish operators. Prices support in connection with fish is a little different from prices support in connection with agricultural products. About 70 per cent of our fresh fish goes to the United States, whereas our dairy products are almost all consumed in Canada.
The United States congress is being faced with what might be called a lobby by some New England congressmen to impose a quota or to raise the tariff on imports of fish. That would be disastrous for our east coast fisheries. We feel that if we moved into prices support at this time those who are trying to bring about tariff increases would say that our fish was being produced under government subsidy and so restrictions against our fish would be justified. With that in mind the fishermen and the industry, appreciating the situation, did not press for prices support, but asked for a further review of the situation in June.
The hon. member for Gloucester raised the question of licences for oyster beds. We have to have some form of control over the areas leased as oyster beds. The licence fee of $1 per acre is just about sufficient to cover the cost of administration.
The hon. member for Charlotte made some flattering remarks about the work done by the dietitians in our kitchen. The fishing industry is appreciative of what these dietitians have done in creating an interest in fish in our schools, restaurants and hotels across the country. He also mentioned the very happy relations which exist between this department and the United States fish and wildlife department. It is a very important thing that these good relations be maintained because our fishermen, Canadian and United States, jointly exploit the two main fisheries of our coasts, north Atlantic and north Pacific, and we of course are very heavily dependent on the United States market. We have had the very best of relations with the United States. International treaties control the fisheries on both our coasts. They work well, and are real examples of international co-operation.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South made a very brave suggestion when he suggested that I should take our dietitians up to the cooks in the parliamentary restaurant and tell them how to cook fish. It would take a

very brave man to tell any cook how to do his job. I thought that when I arranged for the restaurant committee of the House of Commons to come over to our kitchen and see how our girls cook fish they would take the matter into their hands, and next spring when our next session starts they may deal with the matter in the way suggested by the hon. member for Cape Breton South.
The hon. member for Queens raised the case of the Winnie Anne. The premier of Prince Edward Island made a personal intervention in this case about three months ago, as did my parliamentary assistant. The Winnie Anne was a ship built with the assistance of our government subsidy, which became an outright grant if the ship fished for five full years from the time of the subsidy. The Winnie Anne did prosecute the fishery vigorously, but the ship was actually lost three months before the five years expired. The insurance company sent the insurance cheque to the captain of the boat. As far as the law was concerned the ship had not fished the full five years, and so the subsidy was not a gift and the federal government could recover the subsidy out of the insurance. Part of the trouble was that we never got our hands on the cheque. We certainly could not remit anything without having received something. When the owner was up here two or three weeks ago he was persuaded to turn the cheque over, and then I made a submission to treasury board, pointing out that the Winnie Anne had not only prosecuted the fisheries but had done so very vigorously, fishing both summer and winter, and had certainly carried out the spirit of the agreement. The treasury board has approved the payment of the subsidy to the owner.
The hon. member for Annapolis-Kings and the junior hon. member for Halifax both raised this very difficult problem of limits for trawlers and for smaller draggers. Trawlers are a very effective way of catching fish. We must raise the catch per fisherman to raise the economic status of the fishermen. We are keeping our trawlers out beyond the twelve miles for the very reason the hon. member for Annapolis-Kings pointed out, hoping that we can persuade the United States by our example to keep their trawlers out that distance and leave our inshore fisheries for the smaller draggers and for the inshore fishermen using lines.
The junior hon. member for Halifax raised the other problem of the smaller dragger. We have encouraged fishermen and groups of fishermen to build the smaller draggers, as they are a very effective way of catching fish in the inshore regions. Naturally there have been disputes between those who have turned to draggers and those who are still following
Supply-Fisheries
the old methods of inshore fishing. Without dwelling on the merits of the various types of catching fish, I can say that the dragger is now an accepted part of the pattern of modem fishing. It has stabilized the industry, and provided year-round employment in many communities, and for some it has been the salvation of the fishing industry.
However, inshore fishing, which provides the backbone of so much of Nova Scotia's rural economy, has up to now not generally been susceptible to the utilization of draggers and, in fact, there are many areas which are not suitable for the dragger method of fishing. Until recently St. Margaret bay and one or two other bays along the Nova Scotia shore were fished exclusively by the older methods, but this year draggers moved into these bays for the first time and have raised quite a problem for those who were depending on inshore fishing. We have asked the draggers to refrain from further fishing in these bays this season, and since the problem is new we are turning our protection staff and our scientists on to a study of the situation to see whether or not some reasonable compromise cannot be worked out in these areas for the next season.
The hon. member for St. John's West raised the matter first of all of the provincial government of Newfoundland being unable to announce an insurance scheme through Lloyd's of London. That of course has been the experience on the mainland of Canada, too. The insurance of small boats is so hazardous and requires so much supervision as far as administration is concerned that it was not practical for the private companies.
He mentioned the Walsh committee report. The feeling of our department here is that this report was well worth waiting two years for. It is an extraordinarily able summary of the situation in Newfoundland, and we feel points the way to the rehabilitation of that great industry down there. When I was in Newfoundland I urged the chief justice to make sure that the report would come down before the end of this session so we could do something practical about it, starting this summer. In the estimates we have for the first time $1 million for industrial development along the lines suggested by that report.
The actual program which they envisage is a long-term one. The hon. member for St. John's West very wisely pointed out that things such as co-operative education cannot be done overnight; it is a long, slow process. The modernization of the fishing fleet of Newfoundland, the improvement of fish processing methods, the congregation of the

Supply-Fisheries
many little communities into large central communities, with better facilities-all these things are matters of five or ten years, perhaps; but we are very anxious to get a start this year, and that is the reason this item of $1 million appears in the estimates.
His comments on markets of course were very apropos, because he has told us what has happened to some of the traditional markets for Newfoundland salt cod. Some of the markets such as Brazil simply have not got dollars to buy salt cod. Other markets such as Portugal and Spain have developed great fishing fleets of their own and largely satisfy their own demands now. That is one reason we feel it is important to try to diversify the production of Newfoundland fish into more than salt cod, into fresh and frozen fillets for the Canadian and United States markets as well as salt cod for European markets. Along the south coast of Newfoundland that process has been going on for the last three or four years with marked success.
There will always be, we hope, a good market for salt cod. It is a rather low price market when it is contrasted with the purchasing power of the 170 million people who live in the northern half of this hemisphere. But the aim, at least in the Walsh report, is to market our products in as many forms in as many different markets as possible to give better stability to the industry.
I think these are the main points raised by hon. members so far.
